item.title: Week 3: Clarifying Tukey Depth & Debugging Sweep Algorithm
item.dc:creator: Ridhima Singla
item.description:
Abstract

This week was dedicated to resolving the calculation errors in my Tukey depth algorithm from Week 2, which ultimately required a much deeper dive into the underlying geometry. I discovered that my bugs weren’t just syntactical. They stemmed from a gap in understanding of the Tukey depth measure, which resulted in unconsciously mixing two equivalent, but geometrically distinct, definitions of Tukey depth. By decoupling the “Halfspace” view from the “Projection” view, I was able to fix the initial-count logic of my sweep algorithm and resolve a persistent off-by-one boundary error. With an algorithm setup for Tukey Depth finally in place, I am now naturally transitioning into a deeper dive in the Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) depth as the two share many similarities.

Visualizing Two Views of Tukey Depth

While these two geometric interpretations look completely different, they are mathematically identical. Realizing how they align was the key aspect to fixing the error in my algorithm and strengthening my understanding.

Theoretical Foundations: Understanding the Definitions

  • Core Concepts: The graphs above will play a vital role in understanding the formal definitions of these views.

    • Projection View (Left Side): As suggested by (Tukey 1975) and explained in Dr. Leblanc’s instructional materials, a measure of the depth of a point given a sample in 1D is and this can be generalised to dimensions as: where is the projected sample. Let’s unfold this definition with the help of the graph above.

      • The light blue line represents one possible directional vector. The dashed lines show how the 2D data cloud projects onto that 1D light blue line. The red dot represents our query point’s projected position onto the 1D line. To find the depth on this specific line, we simply count the green dots on the left side and the right side of the red dot, and take the smaller of the two. The final depth of this query point is the minimum 1D depth observed over all directional vectors. This method reduces the multivariate problem into a series of univariate problems.

    • Halfspace View (Right Side): (Rousseeuw and Ruts 1998) outlines that the halfspace Tukey depth of a point relative to a dataset is defined as: where H ranges over all closed halfspaces where the boundary line passes through . Let’s unfold this definition with the help of the graph above.

      • The blue arrow represents the line from the query point ‘y’ (red dot) to one of the data points in the sample. The dashed line shows the result of extending this line to infinity. We observe that this line divides the plane into two spaces, left and right. To find the depth for this specific line, we just count the number of dots (sample points in black) on the left side and the right side of the line, and take the smaller number. The final depth of this query point is the minimum depth observed over all possible lines through the query point.
  • Literature Context: Consulted (Tukey 1975) and (Rousseeuw and Ruts 1998) specifically to extract and understand the definitions discussed above.

Methodological Pivots & Insights

Last week, my single point Tukey algorithm was producing results that completely mismatched the verified ddalpha package output. I spent the week tracing the variables and discovered two distinct logic errors.

  • Error 1: Incorrect Initial Count (Mixing Definitions)

    • The Problem: The sweep algorithm I am writing is strictly based on the Projection definition. However, when I wrote the code to calculate the initial count (the number of points that project on the right side before the angular sweep begins from 0 to 360 degrees), I accidentally wrote logic based on the Halfspace definition. I was counting the total number of observations in the top-half (positive y-axis), instead of counting the total number of observations in the right-half (positive x-axis), which is all the points that project on the right before the sweep begins.

    • The Fix: I was implementing one definition but using the boundary rules of the other. Once I realized that the initial count simply represents all points that initially project onto the right side of the directional vector at angle 0, I rewrote the initialization chunk, and the sweep angles finally aligned.

  • Error 2: Off-By-One

    • The Problem: Even after fixing the sweep, my depth was constantly exactly one less than the ddalpha depth. However, this only happened for in sample points (points that existed in the dataset). When I tested an out of sample point, my code matched ddalpha perfectly.

    • The Fix: Dr. Leblanc helped me understand that it comes down to the definition of a closed halfspace vs an open halfspace. A closed halfspace includes the boundary line itself. In my original logic, I didn’t explicitly count the target point in the left/right totals because I assumed that adding 1 to both sides wouldn’t change which side was the minimum. While it is true that adding 1 to both sides doesn’t change which side is smaller, it definitely changes the final numerical depth value. Because the target point sits on the boundary, it must be counted if considering closed halfspaces. Understanding this helped me realise that ddalpha uses closed halfspaces whereas I implemented the open halfspace definition. Thus, this was not so much of an error but rather a difference in implementations.

Computational Implementation

  • Infrastructure: Continuing in R, utilizing the ddalpha package primarily for output verification.

  • Algorithmic Complexity: By sorting the projected angles before starting the circular sweep, the exact computation of the bivariate Tukey depth was achieved in time.

  • The Corrected Logic (The Initial Count): Following the correct logic of the projection approach, the algorithm isolates the exact number of points projecting onto the right side of the initial directional vector at angle 0 before the sweep begins.

# BUG FIX: Implementing correct projection logic
# Correctly isolating the initial count of points on the right side of the 0-degree vector

#function to check if we are in the right-half (to find initial count)
checkQuad = function(x){
  if(x > 0){
    answer = 1
  } else{
    answer = 0
  }
  return(answer)
}

#calculating starting depth (i.e. initial count)
minDepth = 0
right_count = 0
n = nrow(df)
i = 1
while(i <= nrow(df)){
  if(checkQuad(shiftedMPG[i]) == 1){
    right_count = right_count + 1
  }
  i = i + 1
}
left_count = n - right_count
minDepth = min(left_count,right_count)
  • Note: The complete, executable R script for the bivariate Tukey sweep algorithm is available in the project repository

Future Work

  • Optimize the R syntax in the algorithm by replacing standard loops with vectorized operations to better handle larger datasets and eliminate computational bottlenecks.
  • Scale the corrected single-point Tukey algorithm to compute depth for an entire dataset.
  • Check how the algorithm scales as
  • Begin literature review and implementation for Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) depth.

References

Rousseeuw, Peter J., and Ida Ruts. 1998. “CONSTRUCTING THE BIVARIATE TUKEY MEDIAN.” Statistica Sinica 8 (3): 827–39. http://www.jstor.org/stable/24306466.
Tukey, John W. 1975. “Mathematics and the Picturing of Data.” Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians 2: 523–31.

item.title: Week 2: First Computations in R - Implementing Mahalanobis & Tukey Depth
item.dc:creator: Ridhima Singla
item.description:
Abstract

This week marked the transition from understanding mathematical theory to applying it through computational implementation. The primary goal was to have a functioning algorithm, leaving runtime optimization for later iterations. After reviewing Dr. Leblanc’s notes to solidify the core geometry, I wrote my first R scripts to compute Mahalanobis depth (for an entire dataset) using matrix algebra and Tukey depth (for a single point), understanding why simple distance measurements fail in multivariate space, and learning two different but equivalent ways to compute Tukey depth. While built-in R functions made computing Mahalanobis depth straightforward, I spent the vast majority of my time struggling with the geometric complexities of Tukey depth.

Theoretical Foundations: Two Approaches to Computing Depth

  • The Core Concept: This week focused on two different methods for calculating depth.

    • Mahalanobis depth is based on Mahalanobis distance. It relies on the covariance matrix to measure how central a point is relative to the distribution’s shape and spread.

    • Tukey (halfspace) depth takes a geometric approach. Using the projection interpretation, it determines depth of a point by evaluating the minimum number of data points whose orthogonal projections fall to one side of the origin across all possible directional vectors.

  • Literature Context: Relied primarily on Dr. Leblanc’s notes to solidify the theoretical foundation and understand computational geometry via animations. Briefly referenced (Mosler and Mozharovskyi 2022) for an introduction to Mahalanobis Depth and its properties.

  • Research Curiosities: (Mosler and Mozharovskyi 2022) demonstrates that Mahalanobis depth can be calculated exactly in time for any number of dimensions. However, because this depth method is not robust to outliers, it is unreliable for many modern applications. I am naturally curious to explore robustified versions of Mahalanobis depth. What computational trade-offs must we make when transitioning from the standard version to a robust one?

Computational Implementation

  • Infrastructure & Tools: Exclusively coded in R due to its large variety of built-in matrix operations, and the ddalpha package, which provided functions to verify my algorithm’s outputs.

  • The Approach:

    • Mahalanobis: Due to the simple structure of the formula and the built-in matrix operation functions in R, implementing the algorithm was straightforward and easily extendable to the entire dataset across higher dimensions.

    • Tukey: Of the two definitions, I opted to implement the projection interpretation using a sweep style algorithm. To ensure mathematical accuracy and clarity in understanding, I isolated the algorithm to compute the depth of a single sample point only.

Visualizing the Output

View the Code to Generate the Scatterplot 
#plot data to observe how the depth changes
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(updatedDF, aes(x = updatedDF$mpg, y = updatedDF$wt, 
                      label = updatedDF$mhlnbsDepth_2d)) +
  geom_point() + geom_text(color = "darkred",
                           size = 1.5, vjust = -1)

  • Observation: The most fascinating takeaway from the above Mahalanobis visualization was observing a highly counter intuitive result. I found a specific point (22.8, 2.320) that was physically closer to the geometric center of the data as per Euclidean distance, yet it had a lower Mahalanobis depth than the point (26.0, 2.140) that was physically further away.

  • Understanding Why?: Upon further discussion with Dr. Leblanc, I learnt that this is because the data distribution is elliptical (due to the two variables being correlated) rather than perfectly circular, and depth is determined by the data’s covariance structure.

    • The First Eigenvector (Maximum Variance): Point (26.0, 2.140) lies in this direction. Because the data spreads widely here due to high variance, a point can be physically distant but still maintain a high depth.

    • The Second Eigenvector (Minimum Variance): Point (22.8, 2.320) lies in this direction. Because the data is tightly clustered here due to low variance, moving even slightly away from the center causes the depth to drop drastically.

Methodological Pivots & Insights

Implementing Tukey depth required a major conceptual pivot. My initial idea to interpret the projection definition was to rotate a line in one degree increments to find the minimum depth.

After discussing this with Dr. Leblanc, I realized that this “grid approach” was fundamentally flawed. It only provides an approximation for the depth and not the exact answer. If the true minimum is achieved at a fraction of a degree, the increment approach misses it entirely. Furthermore, it scales poorly as sample sizes grow.

I abandoned the grid approach in favor of the sweep algorithm. Instead of rotating a line, we use linear algebra to compute the exact angles where a point switches from projecting on the right versus the left. By keeping track of the action to be taken at each angle, we can sweep the sorted list of angles one by one, tracking the absolute minimum. This pivot moved my algorithm from an inefficient approximation to computing the exact Tukey depth in 2D.

Current Roadblock

  • The Unresolved Bug: While the transition to the sweep algorithm was conceptually successful, my current R script for the single point Tukey depth is producing an answer that is different from the one computed by the ddalpha package function, even after accounting for the normalization.

  • My Hypothesis: I suspect there is a flaw in how I am tracking the initial right count (i.e. number of points that project on the right of the origin) before we start sweeping the list going from 0 to 360. I have isolated the code chunk that counts the initial count and plan to debug it next week after consulting Dr. Leblanc.

Future Work

  • Debug the logic in the Tukey algorithm to resolve the current calculation error.

  • Scale the corrected single point Tukey algorithm to compute depth for an entire dataset.

  • Introduction to “Integrated Rank-Weighted (IRW) Depth”.

References

Mosler, Karl, and Pavlo Mozharovskyi. 2022. “Choosing Among Notions of Multivariate Depth Statistics.” Statistical Science 37 (3): 348–68. https://doi.org/10.1214/21-STS827.

item.title: Week 1: Defining the Depth Function & Infrastructure Setup
item.dc:creator: Ridhima Singla
item.description:
Abstract 1

I kicked off my 16 week undergraduate research term this week under the supervision of Dr. Alexandre Leblanc by defining the core scope of our project: the statistical and computational challenges of Data Depth. While the week was heavily focused on literature review, foundational theory, and establishing the technical infrastructure to document the progress over the summer, it also allowed me to pinpoint the applications of this concept that I am most interested in exploring. Specifically, I want to investigate how data depth can be used for robust outlier detection under missing data. Is there a depth method that can isolate high quality data points from the noise? Can the approach be generalised to higher dimensions?

Theoretical Foundations: What is Data Depth?

  • The Core Concept: In 1D data, finding a median or identifying an outlier is trivial. However, how does one identify the “center” of a massive, multidimensional dataset? Data depth provides a non parametric approach that builds a center outward ordering of points in multivariate space, allowing us to mathematically define how “deep” or central a specific data point is relative to an entire multidimensional cloud. The higher the depth, the more central is the point within a cloud of data points.

  • Literature Context: Reviewed foundational slide decks and presentations provided by Dr. Leblanc to get a high level introduction to existing depth functions and their properties.

  • Research Curiosities: Moving forward, I am highly interested in exploring the computational bottlenecks of depth algorithms. I am also curious to compare the various depth functions when applied to data with missing observations.

Computational Implementation

  • Infrastructure & Tools: Set up a research log using Quarto and GitHub Pages to document the research progress.

  • The Approach: Configured the local development environment on my computer to handle Python and R computations, ensuring all libraries are properly optimized.

Methodological Pivots & Insights

The first major roadblock I encountered was informational, not technical. While there is a substantial volume of literature on the subject, much of it assumes a high level of prior knowledge, and heavily leans toward advanced applications rather than foundational theory. As a beginner, the challenge was figuring out where to start, identifying foundational readings, and reserving advanced ones for later. To navigate this, Dr. Leblanc helped narrow down a reading list for the initial weeks, allowing me to select a single paper as my starting point.

Future Work

  • Deconstruct the chosen foundational paper.
  • Write the first R scripts to compute Mahalanobis Depth and Tukey Depth for a single point.
  • Paper selected for Review - (Mosler and Mozharovskyi 2022)

References

Mosler, Karl, and Pavlo Mozharovskyi. 2022. “Choosing Among Notions of Multivariate Depth Statistics.” Statistical Science 37 (3): 348–68. https://doi.org/10.1214/21-STS827.
